did_you_know.text: The verse describes the LORD as both the one who wounds and the one who heals: “He has torn us to pieces, but he will heal us; he has struck us down, but he will bind up our wounds.” Thus, returning to him is presented as a path to healing and restoration.
The expression “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” describes hope for renewal after a period of suffering and distress, and for living in the LORD’s presence.
Knowing the LORD is presented as an ongoing process: “Let us know; let us pursue knowing the LORD.” The verse compares his appearing to the dawn and his blessing to rain that refreshes the land.

The words “late rain” and “early rain” refer to different kinds of rain: the late rain falls at the end of the rainy season, while the early rain falls at its beginning. Here, both symbolize abundance and blessing.
The LORD compares the faithfulness of Ephraim and Judah to a morning cloud and dew that quickly disappears. The image emphasizes that their spiritual awakening is neither stable nor lasting.

The LORD says that he cuts down and acts through the prophets, and that the words of his mouth bring judgment. The prophets are therefore presented as messengers who warn the people about their conduct.
The verse emphasizes that faithfulness and knowing God are more important than sacrifices alone: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and acknowledgment of God rather than burnt offerings.”
Israel is described as having broken the covenant and betrayed the LORD. The use of the phrase “like Adam” compares the people’s covenant violation with the breaking of a covenant or moral command.
Gilead is described as “a city of evildoers” and as a place marked by bloody footprints. The verse presents it as an example of a society where crime and violence had become widespread.
A band of priests is described as lying in wait and murdering people on the road to Shechem. The criticism is therefore directed not only at the people but also at those holding religious authority.
A “horrible thing” is found in the house of Israel: prostitution and defilement associated with Ephraim. The language presents the sin as a condition that contaminates all Israel.

Judah is also included in the words of criticism through the image of the harvest. The verse connects Judah’s future with the restoration of the people and with what will be reaped as a result of their actions.
